titulo.en: The door is closed, the light is on

objetivo.en: Describe the condition of the parts of an apartment with estar + participle while visiting it with the landlord.

nota.en: In Ecuador and across Latin America, an apartment is un departamento.
The surface you walk on.
You also hear el cuarto, which means room.
Plural: las luces.

explicacion.en: To say what condition something is in right now, use estar + participle, not ser. English says “is” in both cases, but Spanish needs estar here.
The participle works like an adjective: it agrees with the noun in gender and number. Ventanas is feminine plural, so cerradas.
La luz is feminine, so the participle ends in -a: prendida. The ending changes with the noun, not with the verb estar.

texto.en: To say what condition something is in, Spanish uses estar + a participle. The participle describes the result of an action: someone closed the door, so now la puerta está cerrada. English says “is closed” for both the action and the result; Spanish separates them. For -ar verbs the participle ends in -ado (cerrar → cerrado, ordenar → ordenado, amueblar → amueblado). For -er and -ir verbs it ends in -ido (prender → prendido). The participle works like an adjective, so it agrees with the noun: la ventana cerrada, las ventanas cerradas, el dormitorio amueblado. Remember the difference between action and state: apago la luz means “I turn off the light” (action), and la luz está apagada means “the light is off” (result). Sound tip: the d between vowels in -ado and -ada is soft, like the th in “this”.
The participle changes like an adjective. Tap each form to hear it.

explicacion.en: Daniela is one person, so the pronoun is le. Les is only for more than one person.

texto.en: When you write, pay or send something to someone, Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun. For one person, use le (to him, to her, to you with usted): le pago al casero. For more than one person, use les (to them, to you with ustedes): les mando fotos a mis padres. The pronoun goes before the verb, and you usually repeat the person after a: Le escribo un mensaje al señor Paredes. Remember that a + el becomes al. Me, te and nos work the same way: me escribe (he writes to me), te pago (I pay you), nos manda (he sends us). In English you say “to” or put the person right after the verb; in Spanish the pronoun comes first. The word doy (I give) ends in a sound like the oy in “boy”.
Who gets it? The pronoun goes before the verb. Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: For me, for you, with me, with you

objetivo.en: Divide the household chores and suggest doing something together with para mí, para ti, conmigo and contigo.

nota.en: Sacar la basura = to take out the trash.
Lavar los platos = to wash the dishes.
Spanish uses the singular for clothes in general: la ropa.
The double r is trilled: bah-RREHR.

explicacion.en: With me is one word: conmigo. There is no “con mí”.
With you (tú) is one word: contigo. There is no “con ti”.
After a preposition, Spanish uses mí, not yo: para mí. Yo is only for the subject of a verb.
After para, use mí with an accent. Without the accent, mi means “my”.

texto.en: After a preposition (para, con, de, a), most pronouns are the same as the subject pronouns: para él, para ella, para usted, para nosotros, para ellos, para ustedes. Only two change: yo becomes mí and tú becomes ti. So you say para mí and para ti, never “para yo” or “para tú”. Mí has an accent to tell it apart from mi (my); ti has no accent. With con, these two become one word: con + yo = conmigo and con + tú = contigo. There is no “con mí” and no “con ti”. Sound tip: mí is like “mee”, ti is like “tee”, and the double r in barrer is trilled.
Most pronouns do not change. Yo and tú do. Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: The verb agrees with the thing that bothers you, not with me. Los vecinos is plural, so molestan.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: A Daniela le molesta el ruido.

explicacion.en: To name the person, put a before the name and keep the pronoun: A Daniela le molesta el ruido.
The noise is the subject, so the verb agrees with el ruido: molesta. Do not conjugate the verb with yo.

titulo.en: Verbs like gustar: what bothers you, what you lack

texto.en: Molestar, importar, faltar and interesar work like gustar. The thing that bothers, matters, is missing or interests is the subject, and a pronoun says who feels it: me, te, le, nos, les. In English, “the noise bothers me” has the same structure: el ruido is the subject and me is the person. So Spanish says me molesta el ruido. The verb agrees with the thing: me molesta el ruido (one thing) but me molestan los vecinos (more than one); nos falta una mesa but nos faltan dos sillas. Importar means “to matter” or “to mind”: no me importa = I don't mind. To make clear or to stress who, add a + the person before the pronoun: a mí, a Daniela, al señor Paredes. Keep the pronoun: A Daniela le molesta el ruido.
The pronoun says who. Tap each phrase to hear it.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Se me rompí la llave del baño.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Se me rompió la llave del baño.

explicacion.en: The faucet is the subject, so the verb is rompió, not rompí. Me only says who it happened to.
In this pattern se always comes first: se me, se te, se nos. Never “me se”.
The verb agrees with the thing that broke. Los vasos is plural, so rompieron.
Without se the sentence does not work: Spanish says se nos acabó el gas for “we ran out of gas”.

titulo.en: Se me rompió: when things happen to you

texto.en: Spanish often tells about an accident or a surprise as if the thing did it by itself, and the person it happened to is shown with a pronoun: se me rompió la llave del baño = “the bathroom faucet broke on me”. The pattern is se + me, te, le, nos or les + a verb in the third person. The thing is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: se me rompió el vaso (one glass) but se me rompieron los vasos (more than one). Se always comes first: se me, never “me se”. Nobody is blamed, which makes it polite when you explain a problem to the landlord. Three very useful verbs: romperse (to break), dañarse (to break down) and acabarse (to run out). With a name, add a: a Daniela se le rompieron los vasos. To say what the result is, use estar + participle, as you learned earlier in this block: se nos dañó el refrigerador, and now el refrigerador está apagado. Sound tip: the ñ in dañó is like the ny in “canyon”.
